## Introduction

Anthropogenic global changes such as land-use change, resource exploitation, climate change, invasive alien species, and pollution pose major and accelerating threats to biodiversity and ecosystem functioning [@Ipbes2019-sd]. These global change drivers do not act in isolation but occur simultaneously and often interact in complex ways so that their net impacts may exceed the sum of single drivers [@oliver2014interactions; @Komatsu2019-yr; @rillig2019role; @Speiser2022-st; @xue2024number]. Given these complexities, forecasting changes to biodiversity requires an understanding of the mechanisms underlying the multifactorial and interactive nature of anthropogenic global change drivers.

A growing literature suggests that different global change drivers can affect plant community diversity and composition in grasslands through a similar underlying mechanism: changes in community biomass that shift the intensity and nature of the dominant plant-plant interactions [@borer2014herbivores; @li2024water; @klein2004experimental; @collins2022global; @tylianakis2008global]. For example, warming and nitrogen addition typically increase community biomass in productive habitats such as temperate or alpine ecosystems, which may lead to communities with taller, faster growing species leading to biodiversity loss due to competitive exclusion of subordinate species [@Alexander2015-gu; @Vandvik2020-hu; @wust2021interaction]. A few studies have explicitly shown that this increased competitive exclusion with increased biomass is for light [@eskelinen2022light; @hautier2009competition]. In contrast, grazing removes biomass [@frank2005interactive; @Bernes2015-yg], which can lead to increased diversity, particularly in more productive habitats [@Austrheim2001-nu; @frank2005interactive; @niedrist2009plant; @Bernes2015-yg; @borer2024planning; @proulx1998reversal]. Accordingly, grazing has been shown in some cases to reverse the effects of warming and nitrogen addition, thus preventing species loss [@kaarlejarvi2017herbivores; @klein2004experimental; @post2008opposing; @song2020grazing].

While these studies suggest that biodiversity responses to different global change drivers often operate through the same indirect mechanisms: notably change in the magnitude and nature of plant-plant competition for light and resources, as reflected by change in community biomass, this hypothesis has rarely been tested in a unified way. @white2014direct studied direct and indirect effects of different drivers on plant diversity in three temperate grasslands and identified shoot biomass as a key indirect driver of species loss in response to grazing and precipitation. @Vandvik2020-hu showed that complex interactions of temperature and precipitation change could be simplified by including the biomass of novel species as a proxy of plant-plant interactions. Building on these findings, we propose that global change drivers can affect plant diversity directly or indirectly via community biomass that changes the dominance of plant-plant interactions (@fig-concept a, b). If so, changes in community biomass provide a *common currency* to quantify the magnitude of multiple global change drivers. Using community biomass as a mechanistically linked mediator simplifies analysis by avoiding the more complex task of understanding how individual species interactions change across environmental contexts and global change drivers. Instead, biomass acts as a proxy for shifts in dominant plant–plant interactions (i.e. competitive interactions or facilitation).

We hypothesize that climate warming, nitrogen addition, and grazing affect diversity and species composition via impacts on community biomass. Specifically, in mountain ecosystems that are temperature and nutrient limited, we expect warming and nitrogen addition to increase community biomass, leading to an increase in the intensity of competition for light and nutrients, and hence an increase in competitive exclusion. Grazing should have the opposite effects. Alternative mechanisms independent of plant-plant competitive interactions are also possible. For example, climate warming may shift conditions beyond or into the climate niche of some species, which may therefore go locally extinct or successfully colonise [@nomoto2021drivers]. Second, increased nitrogen addition, especially at high levels, can lead to soil acidification [@tian2015global], which can lead to shifts in species composition and diversity due to differences in tolerance to acidic conditions. Similarly, some species may have traits that make them particularly tolerant or intolerant to direct effects of grazing [@archibald2019unified], leading to community shifts not mediated through biomass. To further aid the interpretation of shifts in composition, and diversity, we use ecological indicators of species' responses to the environmental conditions [@diekmann2003species; @rumpf2018range], and calculate community weighted mean indicator values to provide further insights into the potential mechanisms underlying these dynamics.

To test the generality of biomass as a mediator of indirect global change effects, we conducted multi-factor global change experiments, along an elevational gradient in mountain grasslands, including an alpine and sub-alpine plant community (@fig-methods). Mountains are an ideal natural laboratory to study global change impacts, because plant community responses to global change drivers often vary along environmental gradients and across habitats [@milchunas1993quantitative; @elmendorf2012plot; @Humbert2016-wg; @bjorkman2018plant; @Vandvik2020-hu; @tito2020mountain]. We therefore manipulate three common global change drivers in a field experiment that are known to be limiting factors in this system \[at least W and N!\]: climate warming, nitrogen deposition, and clipping or natural grazing, and replicated these experiments in an alpine and sub-alpine grassland community in Western Norway (@fig-methods).
